A logical qubit was just measured on its own inside a QLDPC code block, on real hardware.

A team including UCL and the UK's NQCC ran QLDPC surgery on a [[10,2,3]] generalised bicycle code on Quantinuum's H2-2.

Single-round measurement of logical X1: 0.72% error.

Quantinuum ($HON) cut ion-trap logical qubit measurement error to 0.72% using generalized bicycle codes—crossing the critical 1% fault-tolerance threshold and slashing physical qubit overhead compared to standard surface codes.

Quantinuum + Sandia ran the first full tomography of a universal logical gate set: 1 logical qubit in 7 ions on H1, T gate included.
After QEC, errors looked mostly random; an emulator also caught small coherent over-rotations (arXiv). @QuantinuumQC @SandiaLabs #QuantumComputing https://t.co/zmnMHcRtiP

The number developers should watch in error correction is Λ.

It tells you how much the logical error rate drops each time the code distance goes up by 2.

On Google's Willow chip, Λ = 2.14.
Their 101-qubit, distance-7 surface code hit 0.143% logical error per cycle.

urls.description: PQI Collaborative Seminar / DINS Seminar talk by Prof. Filip Rozpedek of UMass Amherst. Title: Scalable entanglement distribution using quantum repeater chains with error correction Abstract: In this talk I will provide an overview of our recent efforts in designing resource-efficient quantum repeater architectures with error correction. In the first part of the talk, I will focus on memory-based architectures, where we argue that repeater chains with error-correction capabilities should exploit more than one physical platform, combining the complementary strengths of different quantum memory technologies into a single hybrid repeater architecture. An important constituent of such an architecture is a hybrid repeater which combines type-1 memories, characterized by fast entanglement generation rates and suitability for multiplexing, and type-2 memories that offer long coherence times and low two-qubit gate error rates.
